items.stem: Explain why astronomers use light-years rather than kilometres for distances between stars.
items.answer: The distances are so large that kilometres give unmanageably huge numbers; a light-year is about 9.5 × 10¹² km.

items.stem: Explain why we see distant galaxies as they were in the past.
items.answer: Light takes millions or billions of years to reach us, so the light we see left the galaxy long ago.

items.stem: Astronomers measure the speed of a galaxy moving away from the Milky Way as 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) State one other piece of evidence for the Big Bang. (b) Estimate the age of the Universe from H₀ and state an assumption.
items.answer: (a) Cosmic microwave background radiation. (b) 1/H₀ ≈ 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years; assumes constant expansion rate.

items.stem: Explain why a main-sequence star stays stable for billions of years.
items.answer: The outward pressure from the hot gas (from fusion energy) balances the inward pull of gravity.

items.stem: Explain why elements heavier than iron are thought to form in supernovae.
items.answer: Fusion in stars can build elements only up to iron; the huge energy of a supernova explosion makes heavier nuclei, which are scattered into space.

items.stem: Rigel is a blue supergiant. State the stage of its life cycle it has reached and predict what will happen to it next, giving a reason.
items.answer: Blue supergiant; next: supernova, because its fate depends on its mass.

items.stem: Astronomers study a main-sequence star with 30 times the mass of the Sun. (a) Explain why the star is stable during its main-sequence stage. (b) State the main source of the star’s energy.
items.answer: (a) Outward thermal pressure balances the inward gravitational force. (b) Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.

items.stem: A star of about 8 solar masses has just formed from a nebula. (a) Describe how the star formed. (b) Explain why elements formed in stars end up in planets.
items.answer: (a) Gravity pulled gas and dust in a nebula together; the protostar heated up until fusion of hydrogen began. (b) Supernovae scatter heavy elements into space; they join later nebulae that form new stars and planets.

items.stem: Compare the life cycles of a star like the Sun and a star 20 times more massive, explaining why their end points differ.
items.answer: Both form from a nebula and spend most of their lives fusing hydrogen on the main sequence. The Sun-like star becomes a red giant, sheds a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf. The massive star burns faster, becomes a red supergiant and explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole, because its core gravity is strong enough to collapse beyond the white-dwarf stage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shared stages; 2 marks Sun-like path; 2 marks massive path; 1 mark reason (mass/gravity) – max 5.

items.stem: Explain how redshift supports the Big Bang theory.
items.answer: Light from distant galaxies is redshifted, so they are receding; more distant galaxies have bigger redshift and recede faster, so the Universe is expanding from a single point.

items.stem: Galaxy data (distance / million light-years; recession speed / m/s): C: 200, 4.4 × 10⁶; A: 50, 1.1 × 10⁶; B: 120, 2.6 × 10⁶. Describe the relationship and explain what it suggests about the Universe.
items.answer: Speed is (roughly) directly proportional to distance: further galaxies recede faster. This suggests the Universe is expanding, consistent with the Big Bang.
items.markingKey: 1 mark proportional/positive correlation; 1 mark expansion; 1 mark Big Bang link.

items.stem: Astronomers measure the speed of a galaxy moving away from the Milky Way as 1.1 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) Calculate the distance to the galaxy (H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹). (b) State one other piece of evidence for the Big Bang.
items.answer: (a) 5.0 × 10²³ m (b) Cosmic microwave background radiation.

items.stem: Astronomers measure the speed of a galaxy moving away from the Milky Way as 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) Calculate the distance to the galaxy (H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹). (b) Explain how redshift data support the Big Bang theory. (c) State one other piece of evidence for the Big Bang.
items.answer: (a) 3.0 × 10²⁴ m (b) More distant galaxies recede faster, so the Universe is expanding from an initial point. (c) Cosmic microwave background radiation.

items.stem: A telescope survey measures many galaxies. The distance to the galaxy is reduced to a quarter. Predict, with a reason, how the recession speed of the galaxy changes.
items.answer: The recession speed of the galaxy becomes a quarter.
items.markingKey: Using v = H₀d: recession speed of the galaxy ∝ distance to the galaxy; factor = 0.250 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A spectrum of a galaxy shows its absorption lines shifted towards the red end; its speed of recession is 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s. Calculate the distance to the galaxy (H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹).

A spectrum of a galaxy shows its absorption lines shifted towards the red end; its speed of recession is 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s. (a) Explain what is meant by redshift. (b) Convert the distance to light-years (1 ly = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m).
items.answer: (a) An increase in the observed wavelength of light from a receding source. (b) 3.2 × 10⁸ light-years
